abstract: A phylogenetically diverse suite of modern tooth enamel/enameloid bioapatite from fishes, mammals, and reptiles from 22 species were chemically and structurally analyzed to establish whether crystal structure and chemistry are phylogenetically correlated. Rietveld refinement analysis of x-ray diffraction data suggests variable crystallographic parameters across vertebrates. Coupled chemical data show correlations between the a-axis of bioapatite and the proportions of sodium substitution for calcium, the introduction of vacancies, and carbonate substituting for phosphate (B-type substitution) or channel anions (A-type substitution). Principal component analysis of all variables suggests that a-axis lengths are highly influenced by the introduction of carbonate in both crystallographic sites. Phylogenetic variations in chemistry and structure of enamel/enameloid crystals show how biomineralization processes have changed through evolutionary time with implications for variation in biomineralization processes across vertebrate lineages. The predominant controls on tooth enamel/enameloid crystal structure are phylogeny rather than primary diet or habitat. Crystal structure variations also influence material properties across organisms, which may control how teeth are fossilized.
